https://www.politico.eu/article/giorgia-.text: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said her government is preparing two legislative proposals that would ban face coverings in Italian schools and restrict the number of foreign students allowed in classrooms. “Italian children cannot feel like a minority in the classroom,” she said Sunday in a speech at Fenix , an annual event organized by the youth division of her right-wing Brothers of Italy party. “If the number of children who do not understand the language of instruction becomes large, or even forms the majority, that is no longer integration; that is neglect,” Meloni added. Advertisement Advertisement Roughly 930,000 students without Italian citizenship are enrolled in the country’s schools, representing almost 11.6% of the school population, according to research institute Fondazione ISMU. Over the last decade, the number of foreign minors in the country has fallen by 4.5%, ISMU found. Meloni did not elaborate on what her cabinet’s proposed cap on foreign students might entail. The Italian leader came to power buoyed by voters concerned with immigration issues, and made tackling migration a key pillar of her campaign. It’s not the first time Meloni’s government has looked to ban face coverings. In 2025 her party said it had plans to ban the burqa and niqab in all public spaces nationwide, calling the legislation a response to “Islamic separatism.” The bill is still under consideration in the country’s lower house.

https://nineoclock.ro/who-is-siegfried-m.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Siegfried Mureșan, nominated by President Nicușor Dan to become Romania’s prime minister on Thursday, September 17, is a Romanian Member of the European Parliament with more than a decade of experience in European politics. At 44, Siegfried Mureșan is one of Romania’s most prominent representatives in the European Parliament. Nominated by President Nicușor Dan on September 17, he is now tasked with forming a government amid a prolonged political crisis. On the occasion of his 45th birthday, Nine O’Clock extends its best wishes to Siegfried Mureșan. Born on September 20, 1981, Mureșan will turn 45 on Sunday, September 20, 2026. He currently serves as Vice-President of the European People’s Party (EPP) and Vice-Chair of the EPP Group in the European Parliament , the largest political group in the institution. His nomination comes at a challenging moment for Romania, following months of political deadlock and unsuccessful attempts to establish a parliamentary majority. Mureșan has accepted the president’s proposal and faces the task of building a government capable of securing parliamentary support. President Dan cited Mureșan’s experience in the European Parliament and his involvement in negotiating important European dossiers as relevant qualifications for the position. However, the president acknowledged that forming a government would be difficult in the absence of a clearly defined parliamentary majority. Early Life and Education Siegfried Mureșan was born on September 20, 1981, in Hunedoara, Romania. He studied economics at the Bucharest University of Economic Studies (ASE), graduating in 2004. He later continued his academic and professional development in Germany, where he studied European affairs and gained experience in European institutions and policy-making. His early career included work in European public affairs, providing him with experience in the political and institutional environment of the European Union before entering elected office. From European Affairs to the European Parliament Mureșan entered the European Parliament in 2014, beginning a political career that would establish him as one of Romania’s most visible representatives in Brussels. A member of the National Liberal Party (PNL), he is affiliated with the European People’s Party, the centre-right political family that brings together parties from across the European Union. Over the years, Mureșan has taken part in parliamentary work involving economic and budgetary matters, European funding and the EU’s long-term financial priorities. His role within the EPP has also expanded. He currently serves as Vice-President of the European People’s Party and Vice-Chair of the EPP Group in the European Parliament, positions that place him within the group’s political leadership. His European experience has been a central element of his public profile, particularly in discussions concerning Romania’s role in the EU and the country’s access to European funding. Siegfried Muresan in the European Parliament. – Photo Siegfried Muresan on Linkedin A New Challenge in Romanian Politics Mureșan’s nomination as prime minister marks a significant transition from European parliamentary politics to the leadership of Romania’s executive branch. President Nicușor Dan nominated him following consultations with parliamentary parties on September 17, after failing to identify a clearly established governing majority. The nomination followed the collapse of the government led by Ilie Bolojan in May 2026, when a no-confidence motion brought down the administration. Mureșan now faces the challenge of negotiating political support and assembling a cabinet that can obtain Parliament’s confidence. The president has pointed to his experience in European negotiations, while also acknowledging the difficult parliamentary arithmetic facing the nominee. The coming days will determine whether Mureșan can secure sufficient support to form a government and take office. For a politician whose career has largely been shaped by European institutions, the nomination represents a new chapter — one that places him at the centre of Romania’s domestic political negotiations and its ongoing efforts to establish a functioning government. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA View image in fullscreen Scottish first minister John Swinney and his deputy, Jenny Gilruth, at the SNP conference in Aberdeen on 16 October. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA Opinion Scottish independence Why Scottish nationalists should see Burnham as a real threat – and an opportunity Rory Scothorne The PM’s goals may spell bad news for the SNP. Ironically, his EU bridge-building could also resurrect their dreams of independence Sun 1 Nov 2026 04.00 EST Last modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 06.06 EST Share F ifty years ago this month, a group of leftwing Scots gathered in the Golden Lion hotel in Stirling for the inaugural conference of a new political party. The “Scottish Labour party” had formally split from Labour at the beginning of 1976, driven by disillusionment over the party’s timid proposals for a new Scottish assembly. They were led by the firebrand MP for South Ayrshire, Jim Sillars, who promised to take Scotland’s Labour tradition back to its roots in both socialism and home rule. Sillars’ new party was a media sensation in Scotland, and quickly joined by public intellectuals such as Tom Nairn , Hamish Henderson and Neal Ascherson . It offered something new and exciting: a fusion of the two movements that were battling for Scotland’s soul in a decade that had already been defined by electoral clashes between Labour and the Scottish National party. The party struggled, however, to enthuse the working-class voters on whom Sillars had gambled his future. It did attract a handful of Trotskyist activists from the International Marxist Group, and at the October 1976 conference, Sillars orchestrated a heavy-handed purge of the far left, causing proceedings to degenerate into near-violence. At one point, a member of the party’s national organising committee summoned up Ayrshire’s mining heritage against the “entryist” threat, yelling: “We should get our fucking pit boots on and wade into them!” Andy Burnham was not quite as forthright earlier this month, when, midway through the SNP’s conference in Aberdeen, he delivered his own speech in Motherwell , offering to cooperate on further devolution within Scotland. The conference itself was far more peaceful, the SNP having already shed its “fundamentalist” wing with the breakaway of Alex Salmond’s Alba party (which Sillars, it’s worth noting, also endorsed ). The National Economic Council meeting on Friday between Burnham, John Swinney and the Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, emphasised the shared agenda of three governments seeking to combine devolved power with reindustrialisation – precisely what the SLP was calling for in 1976. But the SLP, which never recovered from its public meltdown in Stirling, made another contribution to the cause that matters intensely to the relationship between Burnham and the SNP. Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon Jenkins Read more Keen to make national self-determination palatable to socialists, Sillars’ party sought to remove any hint of separatism from its politics by embracing the new European Economic Community, arguing for “independence in Europe”. With goods, people and services moving freely across borders, independence would no longer mean separation, but simply real equality between self-governing, co-dependent nations. View image in fullscreen Jim Sillars, centre, visits a factory while campaigning in the Glasgow Govan byelection in 1988, which he won for the SNP. Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty Images After the SLP’s collapse, Sillars found his way into the SNP, rising through the ranks to become deputy leader in 1991. “Independence in Europe” came with him. The SNP made some of its first breakthroughs in the 1970s as a Eurosceptic party, distinguishing itself from the three pro-EEC Westminster parties by campaigning against membership in 1975 with the slogan “No voice, no entry”. But by the 1990s, it had completely reversed this position, helped by the new European Union’s growing emphasis on the rights of small nations and minority cultures. The SNP’s newfound Europeanism reflected and reinforced that of the country it came to govern. It was helped, too, by Scotland’s tendency to define itself against English politics, which became more Eurosceptic over the same period. When the SNP’s success produced a referendum on independence , Europe was one of the central issues. An independent Scotland, voters were told, would be a new state, and would therefore have to reapply to join the EU. Scots voted against independence partly to protect their European passports. Two years later, they voted overwhelmingly to remain in that larger union too . But England, with 10 times Scotland’s population, swung the result the other way. Scotland was thus asked, over the period of just two years and two votes, to choose between its membership of the UK and of the EU – but in the wrong order. Immediately after the Brexit vote, support for independence briefly surged, but then dropped. Scots realised they did not fancy yet another wrenching break-up. It was only with the arrival of Boris Johnson as prime minister, the conclusion of a hard Brexit, and the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic that “yes” moved into a consistent lead. Today, yes and no are neck and neck , but many independence campaigners remain concerned about how another referendum campaign might unfold. The fundamental political case for independence has always been that British politics is overwhelmingly Anglocentric, and Scotland’s interests are marginalised. While Brexit has deepened this structural complaint, it has also transformed the economic arguments against independence: if Scotland were to vote for independence and rejoin the EU tomorrow, it would suddenly face a hard border with the rest of the UK, which buys more of Scotland’s exports than every other country in the world put together – including the whole EU. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Some nationalists argue that, under such circumstances, Scotland could be granted the same status as Northern Ireland, which has found a middle ground between European and UK markets. But Northern Ireland has been given special treatment because of the simmering threat of a return to open conflict over the partition of Ireland; Scotland is not a remotely serious candidate for civil war over its borders with England or Europe and would be highly unlikely to be treated with the same sensitivity by the global community. Scottish nationalism’s problem is also its greatest selling point: it is not motivated by any deep ethnic grievance, and as such its supporters are hard to mobilise into the kind of bloody-minded self-sacrifice that might justify some deeper rupture with England. It is founded, instead, on a modern, peaceful and democratic discontent with Westminster’s gradual abandonment of everything that seemed to make Britain worthwhile: good jobs, functioning public services, international cooperation and a vaguely shared moral compass. Burnham is therefore a meaningful threat to the SNP, for this is precisely the nostalgic vision of Britain that he promises to restore – with messaging skills that can finally rival the SNP’s and promises of “ regional empowerment ”. Yet it offers an opportunity as well. It is hard to imagine that Burnham, whether he has three years in power or a decade, will truly be able to resurrect the lost world of dignified work, British industry and social security that he conjures up in his speeches. But it looks increasingly plausible that he may have to rebuild some of Britain’s relationships with Europe as a precondition of his wider agenda. That would repair the one bridge that Scotland truly needs intact for a successful sprint towards independence, should the rest of Burnham’s project falter. https://hvg.hu/vilag/20261112_new-york-b.text: A hatóságok szerint többen a háromszintes lakóépület romjai alatt rekedhettek. Nyolc halottja és tizenhét sérültje van annak a házomlásnak, amely New York Brooklyn városrészében történt – közölték a helyi hatóságok. Lillian Bonsignore, a New York-i tűzoltóság vezetője elmondta: a sérültek között hét gyerek van, négy ember állapota életveszélyes. A hatóságok egyelőre nem tudják, hányan tartózkodhattak az épületben a katasztrófa idején, illetve vannak-e még a romok alatt. A háromszintes lakóépület helyi idő szerint szerda délután omlott össze a Brooklyn déli részén fekvő Flatbush negyedben. A romok jelentős része a szomszédos építési terület munkagödrébe zuhant. A városi építésügyi hatóság szerint az épület mellett éppen földmunkák folytak egy új beruházás előkészítéseként, de egyelőre nem tudni, hogy ez szerepet játszott-e a szerencsétlenségben. A mentési munkálatokban mintegy 250 tűzoltó és katasztrófavédő vesz részt kutyák segítségével. A hatóságok szerint a romok instabil állapota miatt rendkívül veszélyes a beavatkozás. Zohran Mamdani, New York polgármestere azt mondta, hogy a mentőegységek rendkívül nehéz és gyorsan változó helyzettel állnak szemben, mert az instabil romok között kell mozogniuk, amelyek felszíne alatt veszélyes üregek találhatók. A helyi média beszámolói szerint több embert órákkal az omlás után sikerült élve kimenteni a romok alól, köztük egy várandós nőt is. A tűzoltóság szerint a teljes átvizsgálás több napig is eltarthat. Keménydiszkontosodik az Aldi és ezt szebben becsomagolva hivatalosan is bejelentette. Megkérdeztük a vásárlókat, hogyan látják a változó üzleteket.
